---
title: 16. Putting spatial data in context
---

::: {.callout-info}
Maptile services and OpenStreetMap generally will have required attributions you
need to give if you publish maps with their tools. Check the details of
whichever services you use to see how to comply with this.
:::

## Basemaps

Put your map on a map. There are lots of options; Google Maps and OpenStreetMap
are both very popular for map tiles, but they contain a lot of colors and
symbols. For data visualization, simple grayscale or black & white basemaps work
well, like the map tiles from Stamen (now distributed through Stadia) and Carto.
These often require an API key.

In the past, I've mostly used the `ggmap` package, which was designed to be very
easy to use with ggplot, but it doesn't seem to be kept up to date as much and
still points to several providers that are defunct. The newer `basemaps` package
has more updated map providers, so we'll lean towards that. Call
`basemaps::get_maptypes()` to see them all.

Maptiles are generally in web Mercator projection, and to use them with
`basemaps` and `ggplot` with other layers, you'll need to transform your
additional data to CRS 3857.

### Getting and saving API keys

Many services require API keys to use. API keys can be tricky to get and store,
and some, like Google Maps, require you having a credit card on file even if you
only stay within the free tier. Even for a service that doesn't seem like
someone could cause any trouble with it, you want to treat your API keys like
passwords---it's a good habit to get into. Many packages that use APIs will have
functions to help you save your key, and they'll generally save to a specific
[environment
variable](https://kinsta.com/knowledgebase/what-is-an-environment-variable/).
For example, `tidycensus::census_api_key` will save your key to the environment
variable `CENSUS_API_KEY`, and that's where its functions will also look for the
key when you make API calls. `ggmap` has a function to do this for you;
`basemaps` does not, so we'll have to save keys ourselves.

Storing a key as an environment variable allows you to use a secret value (the
key) without explicitly using it in your code. It's common to store environment
variables in a file called `.Renviron`, usually saved to your computer's home
directory rather than the project repo, which gets read every time you start an
R session on that computer. You can edit it manually, or the function
`usethis::edit_r_environ` also helps you find and edit this file. If you do need
to store environment variables in a project, make sure that file (".Renviron" is
default for R, ".env" is common in other languages and with R as well) is
**listed in your .gitignore file** so it stays out of git tracking.

Of the services preset in `basemaps`, you can use these AFAIK without a credit
card:

#### Services that require an API key

- Maptiler
- Stadia (which now provides Stamen maps too)
- Thunderforest
- ~~Carto (recently changed to require an API key, crashed a lot of published maps including some of mine)~~
  can't get it to accept my API key, maybe you'll have better luck

#### Services that don't require an API key

- OSM
- ESRI, surprisingly

Mapbox claims to need a billing address even though I don't have a payment
method set up. You can also add new maptile sources but I haven't tried it yet.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(ggplot2)
library(sf)

qual_pal <- rcartocolor::carto_pal(name = "Vivid")
seq_pal <- RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(n = 5, name = "RdPu")
```

```{r}
#| label: basemap-1

# reproject and use a buffer to get some space around the city
balt_sf <- justviz::tracts_sf |>
    dplyr::filter(county == "Baltimore city") |>
    sf::st_transform(3857)

balt_buff <- balt_sf |>
    sf::st_union() |>
    sf::st_transform(2248) |>
    sf::st_buffer(dist = 1 * 5280)

# back to web mercator for getting maptiles
balt_bbox_merc <- balt_buff |>
    sf::st_transform(3857) |>
    sf::st_bbox()

# back to latlon for osm data
balt_bbox_latlon <- balt_buff |>
    sf::st_transform(4269) |>
    sf::st_bbox()

# I've put this key in an envvar in ~/.Renviron
# so I don't need to expose it in my code
basemaps::basemap(
    balt_bbox_merc,
    map_service = "osm_stamen",
    map_type = "toner_bg",
    map_token = Sys.getenv("STADIA_TOKEN"),
    verbose = FALSE
)
```

That makes a plot, but doesn't return an object we can work with further. Other
functions in the package will return ggplot- and terra-compatible objects.

```{r}
#| label: basemap-gg-1

# basemap_ggplot returns a readymade ggplot object
toner_bg_plot <- basemaps::basemap_ggplot(
    balt_bbox_merc,
    map_service = "osm_stamen",
    map_type = "toner_bg",
    map_token = Sys.getenv("STADIA_TOKEN"),
    verbose = FALSE
)

class(toner_bg_plot)

# basemap_gglayer returns a ggplot layer that could be added to a plot
# seems less likely to be useful
toner_bg_layer <- basemaps::basemap_gglayer(
    balt_bbox_merc,
    map_service = "osm_stamen",
    map_type = "toner_bg",
    map_token = Sys.getenv("STADIA_TOKEN"),
    verbose = FALSE
)

class(toner_bg_layer)

toner_bg_plot +
    # if you find the basemap too harsh, block it out a little
    # with a translucent rectangle
    # annotate(xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, geom = "rect", color = NA, fill = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_sf(
        data = sf::st_union(balt_sf),
        fill = NA,
        color = qual_pal[1],
        linewidth = 1
    )
```

## OpenStreetMap data

OpenStreetMap is an incredible service run by an international nonprofit and
many, many volunteers. They run [lots of interesting
projects](https://openstreetmap.us/) geared towards all different types of
people, not just in GIS. You can [get involved](https://learnosm.org) in
curating and editing it; this is especially important in places that might not
have as much data documented or as many advocates as better-resourced areas. For
example, some friends and I once had a little hackathon to help a local group
that was advocating for more play spaces for kids. In a couple hours, we were
able to get more parks, playgrounds, and other recreational areas (soccer
fields, etc) on the map so people could find them and so the group could better
understand access to fun resources for kids. It's so cool!

::: {.aside}
Keeping servers running on limited infrastructure is hard, so sometimes the OSM
servers are down or overloaded. If you get an error that says "HTTP 5xx", where
"5xx" is any number starting with 5, that means there's a problem with the
server, it's out of your control, and you should try again later. It generally
resolves pretty quickly, and has happened a few times while I wrote these notes.
:::

OSM's servers let you bulk download lots of data on hundreds of different things
from country borders to highways to individual park benches. When you get data
from it, you'll definitely want their list of [keys and location
types](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Map_features) open as a reference,
and you might need to tweak your requests a bit to figure out things like the
different types of highways. Once you know what you want, it's pretty
straightforward to get data with the `osmdata` package, which returns all your
shapes as `sf` objects. This is how I made the set of local highways at
`justviz::highways_sf`.

OSM data is great if you don't want an entire basemap, or you want to customize
which locations are shown. (There are paid services that will do this with
basemaps, such as Mapbox and Maptiler). Let's say we're making a map of some of
the EJSCREEN data related to air pollution, and we want to add highways and
major roads but otherwise keep it pretty plain. `justviz::highways_sf` just has
roads classified as motorways and trunks, but for looking more locally,
including primary roads would also be good.

To get data for a certain set of location types, I supply a bounding box, then
add a set of features to query, and then make the request to return `sf`
objects. This will contain some combination of points, lines, polygons (and
multilines and multipolygons). Also take a look at those objects---they contain
tons of metadata (the highway lines have 239 columns!)

```{r}
#| label: osm-data-1
#| eval: false

# this is crashing so I'm actually saving it locally
highways_osm <- osmdata::opq(balt_bbox_latlon) |>
    osmdata::add_osm_feature(
        key = "highway",
        value = c("motorway", "trunk", "primary")
    ) |>
    osmdata::osmdata_sf()
saveRDS(highways_osm, here::here("assets/highways_osm.rds"))
```

```{r}
#| label: osm-data-2

highways_osm <- readRDS(here::here("assets/highways_osm.rds"))

highway_lines <- highways_osm$osm_lines |>
    dplyr::select(osm_id, name, lanes) |>
    dplyr::mutate(lanes = as.numeric(lanes))

# easier to change ej_natl format first
ej_wide <- justviz::ej_natl |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(
        id_cols = tract,
        names_from = indicator,
        values_from = value_ptile
    )

ej_wide |>
    # then right join with shapes
    dplyr::right_join(balt_sf, by = c("tract" = "geoid")) |>
    # then bring it back to an sf object
    sf::st_as_sf() |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = diesel), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
    # force a legend
    geom_sf(aes(linewidth = lanes), data = highway_lines) +
    scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdPu", direction = 1) +
    scale_linewidth_continuous(range = c(0.1, 1))
```

Here we've got tract boundaries from the Census Bureau, exposure to diesel from
EJSCREEN, and location of highways from OSM. Combined, this shows us that the
central and southeast portions of the city have relatively high potential for
diesel exposure, but it doesn't seem like that's entirely due to highways.
Knowing the city, I-95 cuts through downtown and across the southeast corner and
is a major trucking route, but there's also a lot of industrial activity in
southeast Baltimore in close proximity to densely populated neighborhoods like
Highlandtown. We could add industrial areas from OSM data to investigate more.

## Other spatial data

Maybe you want to put other stuff on your map. If there are specific locations
that provide important context, you might try adding a few essential ones (don't
overdo it). Same goes for regional boundaries, major roads, landmarks to help
your reading orient themself, buffers around a location, etc. A few examples
I've done:

- Using dashed lines to mark an area used in some analyses as a proxy for the
  focus region
- Using points to mark locations of jails and prisons for a map about tracts
  incarcerated people come from
- Adding points for bus stops for a map related to access to childcare by public
  transit

## Putting it all together

Here's everything: a basemap, a choropleth, and some additional shapes. We have
a wrinkle, though: out of the box, `basemaps::basemap_ggplot` makes a plot that
uses the fill aesthetic to draw the maptiles, which are just rasters. That means
when you try to make a choropleth on top of it, you'll have problems because
you're trying to use 2 different fill mappings. One way around it would be to
use the `ggnewscale` package to assign multiple things to the fill aesthetic;
another way is to get the maptiles as a `terra` object, which we've seen for
mapping raster data and which doesn't need to create a fill scale. I'll use the
second one here.

Let's make a map that shows the child population in the city, plus public art,
plus has a basemap to orient people.

```{r}
#| label: basemap-choro
#| fig-height: 6

# crop art_sf to just the city boundaries
balt_art <- justviz::art_sf |>
    sf::st_transform(3857) |>
    sf::st_filter(balt_sf)

acs_sf <- balt_sf |>
    dplyr::left_join(justviz::acs, by = c("geoid" = "name"))

toner_bg_terra <- basemaps::basemap_terra(
    balt_bbox_merc,
    map_service = "osm_stamen",
    map_type = "toner_bg",
    map_token = Sys.getenv("STADIA_TOKEN"),
    verbose = FALSE
)


ggplot() +
    tidyterra::geom_spatraster_rgb(data = toner_bg_terra) +
    geom_sf(
        aes(fill = ages00_17),
        data = acs_sf,
        alpha = 0.7,
        color = "white",
        linewidth = 0
    ) +
    geom_sf(aes(color = "Public art"), data = balt_art, size = 0.75) +
    scale_fill_distiller(
        palette = "RdPu",
        direction = 1,
        na.value = "gray70",
        labels = scales::label_percent()
    ) +
    # use a bigger dot size in legend
    scale_color_manual(
        values = c("Public art" = "black"),
        guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 1))
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(0)) +
    coord_sf(ndiscr = 0) +
    labs(
        title = "Do Baltimore's kids have access to public art?",
        subtitle = "Share of population under age 18 by tract, 2024\nWith locations of publicly-funded artwork",
        color = NULL,
        fill = "% under 18",
        caption = "Sources:\nUS Census Bureau 2024 American Community Survey 5-year estimates\nOpen Baltimore Public Art Inventory, last updated June 2023\nMap tiles © Stadia Maps © OpenMapTiles © OpenStreetMap © Stamen Design"
    ) +
    theme(
        legend.key = element_blank(),
        plot.title.position = "plot",
        plot.caption.position = "plot",
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)
    )
```

[Here's a good blog
post](https://oliverstringham.com/blog/data-visualization/make-maps-with-basemaps-and-insets-ggplot2/)
going over a similar (more polished) procedure and what I used to troubleshoot
this section.

## Combining spatial & nonspatial visualizations

Sometimes the best context is just another chart that can show what you can't do
in a map. This might mean pairing a choropleth to show spatial patterns with a
bar chart to show regional averages, or a map as a snapshot of where things are
now with a line chart of how things got there.

For example, a choropleth of mobility disability rates shows the spatial pattern
locally, with higher rates in East & West Baltimore but closer to the middle of
the city...

```{r}
#| label: mobility-choro

cdc_wide <- justviz::cdc |>
    # dplyr::filter(indicator %in% c("Current asthma", "Annual checkup")) |>
    dplyr::mutate(value = value / 100) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(
        id_cols = c(level, location),
        names_from = indicator,
        values_from = value
    ) |>
    janitor::clean_names()

mobility_choro <- balt_sf |>
    dplyr::left_join(cdc_wide, by = c("geoid" = "location")) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = mobility_disability), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
    scale_fill_distiller(
        palette = "RdPu",
        direction = 1,
        labels = scales::label_percent(),
        na.value = "gray70"
    ) +
    coord_sf(ndiscr = 0) +
    labs(
        fill = "% adults",
        title = "Share of adults with a mobility disability, Baltimore city by tract, 2023"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

while a bar chart contextualizes the city's data...

```{r}
#| label: mobility-bar

mobility_bar <- cdc_wide |>
    dplyr::filter(
        location %in%
            c(
                "US",
                "Maryland",
                "Baltimore city",
                "Baltimore County",
                "Anne Arundel County",
                "Howard County"
            )
    ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
        location = forcats::as_factor(location) |>
            forcats::fct_reorder(mobility_disability)
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(
        x = mobility_disability,
        y = location,
        fill = location == "Baltimore city"
    )) +
    geom_col(width = 0.8) +
    scale_x_continuous(
        expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
        labels = scales::label_percent()
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = seq_pal[3], "FALSE" = "gray50")) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "none", axis.ticks.y = element_blank()) +
    labs(
        title = "Share of adults with a mobility disability by location, 2023",
        x = "% adults",
        y = NULL
    )
```

and a scatterplot shows how it relates to other issues.

```{r}
#| label: mobility-scatter

mobility_scatter <- cdc_wide |>
    dplyr::inner_join(justviz::acs, by = c("location" = "name", "level")) |>
    dplyr::filter(
        level == "tract",
        county %in%
            c(
                "Baltimore city",
                "Baltimore County",
                "Anne Arundel County",
                "Howard County"
            )
    ) |>
    # too many variables
    dplyr::select(location, county, mobility_disability, no_vehicle_hh) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
        is_balt = forcats::as_factor(county) |>
            forcats::fct_other(
                keep = "Baltimore city",
                other_level = "Nearby MD counties"
            )
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = mobility_disability, y = no_vehicle_hh, color = is_balt)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(seq_pal[4], "gray40")) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
    labs(
        x = "% adults with mobility disability",
        y = "% households w/o vehicle",
        color = NULL,
        title = stringr::str_wrap(
            "Share of households without a vehicle (2024) vs share of adults with a mobility disability (2023), by tract in Baltimore city & surrounding counties",
            width = 75
        )
    )
```

```{r}
#| label: mobility-combo

mobility_choro
mobility_bar
mobility_scatter
```
